name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Alderwatch, Valedorn Crown`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Rogue   — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

ACTIVE SCENE — Guard · ENGAGED
The staff on his back was new in a way the road was not. It had come with the robes sometime in the last unmeasured while, along with the knowledge of what it was—light ashwood, a hairline seam of silver down its length—and the memory of Earth had no place to file either one. The grass gave way to packed dirt, the verge narrowed, and the road to Alderwatch took him. Cart ruts ran deep and old toward the walls. Traffic thickened as he walked: a farmer with a loaded handcart, two women driving geese with sticks, a mule train led by a boy who whistled through his teeth. Nobody looked at him twice. A traveler in plain robes with a staff on his back was the kind of thing this road saw every morning. The walls grew as he came on—gray stone, patched in places with newer, paler masonry, high enough that their shadow reached the road before the walls themselves were close. The gate stood open, a double arch with the leaves drawn back, and a line of people and beasts shuffled through it in no particular hurry. Two guards in the city's colors stood under the arch, talking to each other more than watching anyone. Beyond the gatehouse, smoke rose from a hundred chimneys, and voices and hammer-blows carried thin on the wind. The queue moved. A carter ahead of him paid something small into a guard's palm without a word being exchanged, and rolled under the arch. When Alaric's turn came, the nearer guard gave him a glance—the staff, the face, the road dust on his hem—then tipped his chin toward the arch. "In or out, robed one. You're holding the line." Morning traffic pressed at his back. Through the gate, a cobbled street ran into the city between timber-fronted buildings, a tavern on the near corner with its shutters just being unbarred, a smell of bread somewhere close by.

extra.display_text:
"Coming in," he said, and the guard was already turning to the carter behind him. Under the arch the air changed—cooler, smelling of stone and old smoke—and sound closed in around him. extra.display_text:
"Morning." The clerk set her quill down in its holder and gave him her whole attention, which had a practiced, unhurried quality to it. Up close she was younger than the spectacles suggested, with an ink stain worked into the side of her right hand. "Registration's two silver. Once, not yearly." She said it the way people say prices they've said a thousand times. "You sign the roll, put your hand on the measuring stone so we know what to write for strength, and you're done. Guild Rank starts at Novice for everybody—that's your standing with us, what work you're allowed to take. The stone gives the other thing. Power Rank, F through S. We read it off, we don't grant it." Her eyes went to the staff slung on his back and came back to his face. "Mage, then. The board's through the back room there—" a nod toward the ajar door past the counter, "—members only. New mages take what everyone new takes: deliveries, watching caravans, pest work. Temple wardens pay steady to keep the upper catacomb galleries cleared, west of the city. Skeletons, mostly. Suits someone who can throw a bolt." She pulled a blank form and a fresh quill toward her across the counter, then stopped with her hand flat on the paper. "Two silver," she said. "You paying, or still deciding?" Behind him, one of the bench women shifted her crossbow and went back to her nails.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
"Morning." The clerk set her quill down in its holder and gave him her whole attention, which had a practiced, unhurried quality to it. Up close she was younger than the spectacles suggested, with an ink stain worked into the side of her right hand.

"Registration's two silver. Once, not yearly." She said it the way people say prices they've said a thousand times. "You sign the roll, put your hand on the measuring stone so we know what to write for strength, and you're done. Guild Rank starts at Novice for everybody—that's your standing with us, what work you're allowed to take. The stone gives the other thing. Power Rank, F through S. We read it off, we don't grant it."

Her eyes went to the staff slung on his back and came back to his face. "Mage, then. The board's through the back room there—" a nod toward the ajar door past the counter, "—members only. New mages take what everyone new takes: deliveries, watching caravans, pest work. Temple wardens pay steady to keep the upper catacomb galleries cleared, west of the city. Skeletons, mostly. Suits someone who can throw a bolt."

She pulled a blank form and a fresh quill toward her across the counter, then stopped with her hand flat on the paper.

"Two silver," she said. "You paying, or still deciding?"

Behind him, one of the bench women shifted her crossbow and went back to her nails.

"Right." She swept the coins off the counter and bit one out of old habit, then set both in a drawer. "Name's already on your intake slip—Alaric. Sign under it." She turned the form toward him and slid it across with the quill. While he signed she reached under the counter and brought up a slab of pale crystal the size of a bread loaf, set flush into a wooden base, and placed it on the counter between them. "Hand flat on the stone. Few seconds, that's all." The crystal was cool under his palm, then not cool—a faint prickling up through the fingers, and a dim glow waking somewhere deep inside it, the color of morning fog. The clerk watched it, squinting, and after a moment nodded once. "F. That's the starting measure for most everyone; nothing to be discouraged about. It climbs with you." She drew the stone back, wrote a line on the form, and sanded the ink dry. Then she took something from a shallow tray—a small rectangular plate of dull metal, stamped with the Guild's crossed-swords mark and a fresh-punched number—and pushed it across the counter to him with two fingers. "Your plate. Don't lose it; replacing one costs more than joining did. It says you're ours, Novice standing. Contracts get taken and closed at a front desk like this one, in any branch, with proof in hand. Nobody outside these walls closes a job or pays one out, whatever a client tells you on the road." She capped her inkwell and nodded at the ajar door past the counter. "Board's through there. Deliveries and caravan work are up top; the catacomb culling postings sit lower on the board, marked for rank. Read what suits and bring your pick back to me." She was already reaching for the next paper in her stack. "Take the slip you want with you. It's not yours till I stamp it."

extra.display_text:
"Both, then." The clerk took the two slips, glanced at them, and inked her stamp—one, then the other—pressing hard enough that the Guild seal bit deep into the paper. She handed them back with a ledger note beside each. "Delivery's a hand-over job. Crates are waiting at Bram's chandlery on Low Street—he knows to expect someone today, or will by the time you get there. Six crates, and mind the top one; consecrated tallow sweats in warm weather and he'll grumble about chipped corners." She dated the ledger line. "Culling slip needs nothing from me but the level cleared. Slip's seal turns ready when the work's done, you bring both back here, and the Guild pays out at this desk. Not before." She looked up from the ledger. "Chapel's an hour west, past the west gate. The wardens keep a man on the chapel stair most days—show him your plate if he asks questions." A beat. "Two jobs in one walk is sensible, not clever. Don't let it make you careless down there; the galleries refill from the deep levels, and the pencil note on that posting is a week old." She took up her quill again, and the next paper in her stack rustled as she drew it near. "Anything else, or are you off to Bram's?"

"Both, then." The clerk took the two slips, glanced at them, and inked her stamp—one, then the other—pressing hard enough that the Guild seal bit deep into the paper. She handed them back with a ledger note beside each.

"Delivery's a hand-over job. Crates are waiting at Bram's chandlery on Low Street—he knows to expect someone today, or will by the time you get there. Six crates, and mind the top one; consecrated tallow sweats in warm weather and he'll grumble about chipped corners." She dated the ledger line. "Culling slip needs nothing from me but the level cleared. Slip's seal turns ready when the work's done, you bring both back here, and the Guild pays out at this desk. Not before."

She looked up from the ledger. "Chapel's an hour west, past the west gate. The wardens keep a man on the chapel stair most days—show him your plate if he asks questions." A beat. "Two jobs in one walk is sensible, not clever. Don't let it make you careless down there; the galleries refill from the deep levels, and the pencil note on that posting is a week old."

She took up her quill again, and the next paper in her stack rustled as she drew it near.

"Anything else, or are you off to Bram's?"

ACTIVE SCENE — Bram · ENGAGED
Low Street announced itself by smell before he found the sign: hot wax and tallow, a sweet burnt scent that hung over the whole row. A chandler's boy was scraping candle drippings off a stone step outside one shopfront, and pointed wordlessly with his scraping knife when Alaric asked after Bram. The chandlery itself was a deep, dim shop with crates stacked to the rafters and a broad man in a wax-spotted apron weighing wicks at the back counter. He looked up, took in the staff and the robes, and grunted. "Guild, then. Good. Those crates have been eating my floor for a week." He wiped his hands and led the way past the counter to where six plain crates sat banded with rope handles, the top one stamped with a small temple mark in black wax. He thumped one with a knuckle. "Consecrated. Keep them dry, keep them upright, and don't let the chapel keeper talk you into carrying them down the catacomb stair for him—that's wardens' work, and the last boy who did came back with his eyebrows gone." He counted the crates again with a flat hand, six, and then looked Alaric over with the frank appraisal of a man used to judging how much weight a customer could shift. "Chapel's an hour west. You walking them out on your back, or will you want the handcart? Cart's two copper deposit, back when the cart comes back—I get it returned, mind, not the chapel keeper's promise. Your choice."

The two copper rang on the counter, and Bram tipped them into his apron pocket without looking at them. "Cart's in the yard." He ducked through a back door and rolled the handcart out front: two iron-rimmed wheels, worn shafts, a coil of lashings hooked over the handlebar. He kicked one wheel and it spun true, with only a faint squeal. "She sings on the turns. Ignore her." Loading went quick work with two backs. The crates were heavier than their size let on, tallow packed dense, and Bram took the ends while Alaric took the middle, stacking them three and three with the temple-marked one on top, lashings cinched down in a cross. When it was done he left go and looked the load over the way he'd looked over Alaric, judging. "That'll hold to the chapel and back if the road doesn't drown you. It rained Thursday; the low stretch past the west gate holds water like a bowl." He gathered the loose rope ends and hung them back on the handlebar. "Keeper's name is Odo. Old fellow, half-deaf since a powder went off wrong near him years back—knock loud at his hut and don't take his shouting for temper." A customer came in behind, wanting tapers, and Bram moved past the counter to see to her, calling the last of it over his shoulder. "Cart back here whenever, shop's open till dusk." The cart sat loaded by the door, shafts down, Low Street's morning trade flowing past the shopfront.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The two copper rang on the counter, and Bram tipped them into his apron pocket without looking at them.

"Cart's in the yard." He ducked through a back door and rolled the handcart out front: two iron-rimmed wheels, worn shafts, a coil of lashings hooked over the handlebar. He kicked one wheel and it spun true, with only a faint squeal. "She sings on the turns. Ignore her."

Loading went quick work with two backs. The crates were heavier than their size let on, tallow packed dense, and Bram took the ends while Alaric took the middle, stacking them three and three with the temple-marked one on top, lashings cinched down in a cross. When it was done he left go and looked the load over the way he'd looked over Alaric, judging.

"That'll hold to the chapel and back if the road doesn't drown you. It rained Thursday; the low stretch past the west gate holds water like a bowl." He gathered the loose rope ends and hung them back on the handlebar. "Keeper's name is Odo. Old fellow, half-deaf since a powder went off wrong near him years back—knock loud at his hut and don't take his shouting for temper."

A customer came in behind, wanting tapers, and Bram moved past the counter to see to her, calling the last of it over his shoulder.

"Cart back here whenever, shop's open till dusk."

The cart sat loaded by the door, shafts down, Low Street's morning trade flowing past the shopfront.

ACTIVE SCENE — Odo · ENGAGED
The axe sound stopped before he was halfway round the hut, as if the man behind it had felt the cart's rumble through the ground. Then a voice came first, loud, from beyond the woodpile. "Tallow! About time. Set them down here — no, not there, HERE, where the sun can't get at them." Odo came out from behind the split logs with the axe still in one fist, a lean old man in a leather apron over a monk's robe, white stubble on his chin and one ear crusted half-shut with old scarring. He had heard the words badly and guessed them well. He looked at the six crates on the cart, counted them with a jab of his finger — one, two, lips moving — and jabbed six times to be sure. "Six. Good, six." He set the axe head-down in the block and slapped chalk dust off his palms. "Bram packs them tight, doesn't he. Well. Off with them, off with them. Stack them against the north wall there, out of the sun — tallow sweats, and sweated tallow burns crooked. And mind the corners, boy, mind the corners, they're chipped easy." He stood back with his arms folded while the unloading was his to watch, and shouted over the work without pause, half to himself. "Chapel needs two hundred a month, do you know that? Two hundred. The dead don't keep the dark off themselves." He squinted at Alaric's robes and staff. "Guild, are you. Hah. Then maybe you're the one for the stair, eh? No — no, that's the wardens' business, never mind me. Wardens' business." Guard B had drifted down from the stair-top and stood at the corner of the hut, spear grounded, watching the crates come off. The last crate came down onto the grass by the north wall, square with the others, the black wax temple mark facing out. Odo walked the stack and touched each corner in turn, all twenty-four, and grunted at the end of it. "Six, whole." He looked up. "That's the lot, then. Unless Bram sent a message with you?"

d.input: "No message from Bram. Delivery's done — who do I tell it's complete, or will the Guild clerk hear it from you?"

actions: NOTHING TO BOOK — Alaric decides nothing the engine resolves in this message; narrate what he says and does, and the world's response.

extra.display_text:
"Ha?" Odo cupped a hand behind his good ear and leaned in. Alaric said it again, louder, and this time the old man got the shape of it. "Tell the clerk nothing, boy, I can't write and he can't read my hand anyway. The wardens' serjeant rides to Alderwatch at quarter-day; he carries my tally. Bram knows how it works." He waved the matter off, then stopped waving and looked at the stack against the north wall, and his face changed. "Done? No — no, it's not done." He jabbed the axe toward the stack. "These aren't done. You've set six crates of consecrated wax against a wall in the open yard. Jackdaws, boys, weather. There's a store under the chapel — lock on the door, dry as a sermon. That's where they go, down the stair and second door on the left. That's where they've gone these forty years." Guard B shifted at the corner of the hut and spoke for the first time, level and unhurried. "He's right. I'll not fetch them for him, mind — my post is the stair. But nothing's touched down there since spring. Carrying six crates down and back is a fair bit of stairs for an old man." Odo folded his arms again and waited, chalk dust still on his palms.

"Ha?" Odo cupped a hand behind his good ear and leaned in. Alaric said it again, louder, and this time the old man got the shape of it. "Tell the clerk nothing, boy, I can't write and he can't read my hand anyway. The wardens' serjeant rides to Alderwatch at quarter-day; he carries my tally. Bram knows how it works." He waved the matter off, then stopped waving and looked at the stack against the north wall, and his face changed. "Done? No — no, it's not done." He jabbed the axe toward the stack. "These aren't done. You've set six crates of consecrated wax against a wall in the open yard. Jackdaws, boys, weather. There's a store under the chapel — lock on the door, dry as a sermon. That's where they go, down the stair and second door on the left. That's where they've gone these forty years." Guard B shifted at the corner of the hut and spoke for the first time, level and unhurried. "He's right. I'll not fetch them for him, mind — my post is the stair. But nothing's touched down there since spring. Carrying six crates down and back is a fair bit of stairs for an old man." Odo folded his arms again and waited, chalk dust still on his palms.

"Show you? I'll do better, I'll come along. Forty years I've fed that stair my knees, it can have them a last time." Odo took a ring of keys off a nail inside the hut and shouted back over his shoulder for nobody's benefit, "Second door on the left, mind, the tallow store, not the coffin loft." Guard B fell in beside the cart as it rolled to the stair head without being asked, spear shouldered now, and looked down the steps. "Two trips, that load. Six crates is three a trip if you want your back tomorrow." He said it the way a man says a thing he has watched break others before. "I'll walk down with you. Not to fetch — to watch. Nothing's been down there since spring that we know of, and I don't care for surprises with the door open." The stair went down under the chapel in a tight spiral, worn hollow in the middle of each tread, the cold coming up stronger with every turn until it was cellar-cold, and then the wall-torch brackets began, unlit, and the light came only from the doorway above and a hooded lantern Guard B lifted off a hook with his free hand. His boots rang. The jackdaws' noise upstairs cut off as if a door had shut on it. The bottom levelled into a short gallery with doors facing across it: a heavy one straight ahead, iron-strapped, and two plainer along the left wall. Odo came puffing at the rear, counting doors aloud — "one — two, there, that's ours" — and went past to fit his key in the second door's lock while Guard B stood in the gallery with the lantern raised, playing its light once down the passage beyond the iron-strapped door, where the dark went further than the light cared to follow. Somewhere down there, faint as a knuckle on wood, something ticked and stopped. The lock turned. Cold, dry air came out of the tallow store, and shelves ran along its walls, old candle-smell soaked into the stone. Odo held the door and jerked his head at the cart's crates waiting up the stair. "Three trips, boy. In they go, corners inward."

QUEST READY FOR TURN-IN — Deliver Warden's Tallow to the Chapel Keeper · All six crates of consecrated tallow delivered intact to Odo, shelved corners-inward in the tallow store and locked; Odo counted six, whole.
Three at a time meant a crate hugged to his chest and one hand flat on the cold stone for the turns, the lantern swinging ahead in Guard B's fist, the worn hollows of the treads catching his heels on every second step. The wax smelled of church inside the crate, candle-smoke and something faintly sweet, and the chalked temple mark rubbed off grey on his forearm. "Left-hand shelves — my left! Old stock forward, new behind. Wax leaves the way it comes in, that's the rule of forty years." Odo stood in the store doorway with the key ring still in his hand, conducting the stacking with his chin. "Hand's width between the stacks. Air wants to move, or it sweats. Corners in, boy, corners in." On the second trip, as the crate came level with the gallery, the dark past the iron-strapped door gave one soft knock, like a knuckle twice on wood, and stopped. Guard B tilted his head at it, held still the space of a breath, then went back to watching the stair. He said nothing at all. The last crate went up on the right-hand shelves, corners inward. Odo walked the row once, pressed a lid with the flat of his thumb, counted under his breath, and grunted. "Six, whole, shelved and locked." The key turned; he tried the handle twice after, the way he did everything, and then started up the stair with both hands on the wall like a man wading a river, offering his knees a running complaint the whole climb. In the yard the midday sun came down hard after the cellar cold, and the jackdaws took up their noise again. Guard B climbed to the stair-top, settled the spear across his knees, and went back to watching the road. Odo squinted at Alaric, chalk dust and sweat on his face. "Well then. Water's sweet here if you're dry — pump's by the hut. And I've bread, if you've the stomach for keeper's bread. A body doesn't haul wax down forty steps for thanks alone."

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
Three at a time meant a crate hugged to his chest and one hand flat on the cold stone for the turns, the lantern swinging ahead in Guard B's fist, the worn hollows of the treads catching his heels on every second step. The wax smelled of church inside the crate, candle-smoke and something faintly sweet, and the chalked temple mark rubbed off grey on his forearm.

"Left-hand shelves — my left! Old stock forward, new behind. Wax leaves the way it comes in, that's the rule of forty years." Odo stood in the store doorway with the key ring still in his hand, conducting the stacking with his chin. "Hand's width between the stacks. Air wants to move, or it sweats. Corners in, boy, corners in."

On the second trip, as the crate came level with the gallery, the dark past the iron-strapped door gave one soft knock, like a knuckle twice on wood, and stopped. Guard B tilted his head at it, held still the space of a breath, then went back to watching the stair. He said nothing at all.

The last crate went up on the right-hand shelves, corners inward. Odo walked the row once, pressed a lid with the flat of his thumb, counted under his breath, and grunted.

"Six, whole, shelved and locked." The key turned; he tried the handle twice after, the way he did everything, and then started up the stair with both hands on the wall like a man wading a river, offering his knees a running complaint the whole climb.

In the yard the midday sun came down hard after the cellar cold, and the jackdaws took up their noise again. Guard B climbed to the stair-top, settled the spear across his knees, and went back to watching the road.

Odo squinted at Alaric, chalk dust and sweat on his face.

"Well then. Water's sweet here if you're dry — pump's by the hut. And I've bread, if you've the stomach for keeper's bread. A body doesn't haul wax down forty steps for thanks alone."

extra.display_text:
Odo pumped the water himself, leaning his whole weight on the handle, and shoved a tin dipper across. The bread came wrapped in a rag — dark, dense, sweetened with something like honey — and a stool got kicked over with his foot for Alaric to sit on outside the hut. "Marked done?" He shouted it across the yard, one hand cupped at his ear until Alaric said it again. "The slip's yours, boy, you did the hauling. I can't write, that's the whole of it — a thumbprint's all I could give you and the clerk won't know my thumb from a dog's." He tore his own hunk of bread and chewed a while. "Serjeant rides quarter-day with my tally, that's for the warden's stores, nothing to do with your Guild paper. You tell the clerk at Alderwatch the six crates came, whole, and Odo took them in. That's all he wants. He knows me, or knows of me, one or the other." He sat down on his own stool with the small grunt of a man landing on a stump he knows well. "Forty steps, that stair. Did you count them? Nobody counts them right." He squinted at Alaric with the bread held halfway to his mouth. "Rode out from Alderwatch this morning on that, did you? Guild work. Huh." He chewed. "There's work under the chapel too, if the Guild sends you for it. Dead work. The wardens stopped burying folk upstairs in the spring because of it, and the parish grumbles, and I keep my mouth shut because it's not a keeper's place. But the stair down the other way — the iron door — that's theirs, not mine, and I'll say no more about it." From the stair-top, Guard B had gone very still, spear across his knees, looking not at the road but down the steps behind him.

Odo waved him off with the rag of bread still in hand and a last shout of "Tell them Odo's well!" that followed him out through the hut. At the top of the yard, past the wall, he looked back. Guard B hadn't moved from the stair-top, but he had turned now, spear lying across his knees, and he lifted two fingers off it — not a wave, more a small flat motion downward, toward the steps behind him — then set the hand back and returned to watching the road. A warning to keep clear, or a farewell. It read as the first. The road west to Alderwatch ran dry and rutted under the midday sun, the hedgerows loud with bees. A carter overtook him halfway, an empty grain wagon rattling, and gave him the nod that strangers on the king's road owe each other and nothing more. The walls of the city rose out of the fields at the hour's turn, and the gate took him in with a bored glance at his Guild plate. The Guild hall was cool after the road, the great room smelling of lamp oil and old paper. Behind the middle counter window the clerk with spectacles looked up from a ledger, recognized the plate, and put out a hand. "Alderwatch delivery, chaplain's tallow, west chapel." Alaric set the slip on the counter, and the clerk drew it under the lamp, turned it, read the seal, and produced a small brass stamp from a drawer. The seal went from active to done with one dull click. "Intact, all six? He counted them?" The clerk looked up over the spectacles. "Then that's settled. Forty copper." Coins came across the counter in a counted stack, two copper short and then the last two added. "Anything else on your book, or are you here to read the board? Fresh slips went up this morning."

Cart escort leaves at first light tomorrow, you'd want to be at the dyers' yard by the east gate before the dew's off. And the eel snappers —" he turned a ledger page, "— the cooperative wants them driven off, not butchered. Drive them back down the river and out of the sluice. Any of the three, take the slip to the counter and I'll mark it taken."

The clerk took the slip back, made a note in the ledger, and stamped it taken with the same brass stamp. "There, it's yours. Nobody else can pin it now." A second slip came across the counter, the seal reading active, and he slid it over beside the first. "Dyers' yard — out the east gate, turn left along the wall, follow the smell. Vats and wet wool, you'll know it before you see it. Ask for Mistress Odell." He set the stamp back in its drawer. "Safe by day, mostly. The trouble's been at the ford crossing, evening and dusk, which is exactly when a loaded cart comes late to Reedford. River road's open ground the whole way — no cover for a man on foot to hide in, which cuts both ways. Carts have been robbed, not killed, so far. They take the dye, the drivers keep their teeth." He straightened the ledger and looked at Alaric properly for the first time. "You're Novice, traveling alone. Odell pays for a guard, not a hero — she'll want to see a plate and a staff and nothing more. First light, remember. She won't wait past it, she loses the day's trade."

ACTIVE SCENE — Carter · SHORT
ACTIVE SCENE — Npc.npccarter_heavyset · SHORT
The beer was thin and slightly sour, but it was wet, and the fire took the evening chill off his back. The dice game had broken up into grumbling and a dispute over two coppers that nobody would admit to losing, and the nearest carter — a heavyset man with a knuckle scarred shiny — gave Alaric's question half an ear while he counted his winnings. "Reedford road? Ran it a fortnight back, hauling hides. Daytime, mind, and we came through the ford by noon." He swept the coppers into a fist. "You're asking about the dye robberies, though. Everyone's asking." "Ford crossing," said an older man by the fire, not looking up from mending a whip lash. "Evening and dusk, that's when they've hit. Four times since the spring, always dye carts, always the same stretch. That's not luck, that's knowing what to watch for." "Could be the dyers' own schedule's too regular," the first carter said. "Could be somebody in Alderwatch tells them what's rolling and when." He shrugged at the looks this got. "Well, how else do they always pick the loaded ones? Nobody robs an empty cart twice." The older man bit his thread and tied it off. "Nobody's seen them proper. Drivers say it happens fast — men out of the willow scrub on the south bank, where the trees come down close to the water, before the cart's halfway across. Four or five of them, bows half-drawn, and a knife-man who does the talking. Polite, by all accounts. 'Unload the vats and keep your teeth.'" He snorted. "They've never hurt a driver yet, but they've never let one keep so much as a rag of the cargo either. And they knew where the guards sat, first job. Told the guard to keep his seat and keep his nose out, and he did, because what's one sword against five men in the trees?" He tested the mended lash against his knee, then glanced up at Alaric's staff. "You're taking Odell's cart, then. Well — cross the ford before the sun's low and you'll likely never meet them. They're not brave, they're patient. There's a difference." The first carter gathered his winnings and stood, stretching. "Or they're patient till the day they're not. Tam's a careful man, though. He'll want to push through early. Listen to him."

The copper went over and the roll and sausage went into his hand, still warm from wherever the landlady kept them. She was already turning back to her porridge pots. "Mistress Odell's cart goes even when it rains," she said, to the pots rather than to him. "You'll not be waited on out there." The east gate streets were still mostly shutters and cats at this hour, the watch lamps being snuffed along the wall. The dyers' yard, though, was awake: the big vat was cold and covered, and the low shed doors stood open, lamplight inside. A cart stood half-loaded in the yard, two squat casks lashed down on the bed with waxed canvas over them, and an old man with white stubble and hands like tree roots was going over the harness buckle by buckle. Tam looked up, took in the staff and the robes, and grunted. "The Guild's mage, then." He went back to the buckles. "Sit on the bench, left side. If I say get down, get down. If I say hold, hold. I don't talk much on the road — I watch it." He tugged a strap, then nodded at the casks. "Load's ready. We roll when it's light enough to see the ruts." Behind him, in the shed doorway, Mistress Odell stood with her arms folded, red-streaked apron already on, watching the yard rather than either of them. She came over as Tam checked the last strap. "Reedford yard, ask for the factor Brantner — he counts the dye and pays the cartage. Tam knows the road." She looked at Alaric, then at the staff. "You crossed through yesterday's muster, so you're paid-for. Ninety copper on delivery at Reedford, Guild pays it, not me — I pay the Guild. So my interest is simple: the vats arrive, the driver arrives, and I'd take it kind if the guard arrives too." She glanced at the greying sky. "It's light enough. Get up, then. And cross the ford before the sun's low, both of you — that's all I'll say on it."

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The copper went over and the roll and sausage went into his hand, still warm from wherever the landlady kept them. She was already turning back to her porridge pots.

"Mistress Odell's cart goes even when it rains," she said, to the pots rather than to him. "You'll not be waited on out there."

The east gate streets were still mostly shutters and cats at this hour, the watch lamps being snuffed along the wall. The dyers' yard, though, was awake: the big vat was cold and covered, and the low shed doors stood open, lamplight inside. A cart stood half-loaded in the yard, two squat casks lashed down on the bed with waxed canvas over them, and an old man with white stubble and hands like tree roots was going over the harness buckle by buckle.

Tam looked up, took in the staff and the robes, and grunted.

"The Guild's mage, then." He went back to the buckles. "Sit on the bench, left side. If I say get down, get down. If I say hold, hold. I don't talk much on the road — I watch it." He tugged a strap, then nodded at the casks. "Load's ready. We roll when it's light enough to see the ruts."

Behind him, in the shed doorway, Mistress Odell stood with her arms folded, red-streaked apron already on, watching the yard rather than either of them. She came over as Tam checked the last strap.

"Reedford yard, ask for the factor Brantner — he counts the dye and pays the cartage. Tam knows the road." She looked at Alaric, then at the staff. "You crossed through yesterday's muster, so you're paid-for. Ninety copper on delivery at Reedford, Guild pays it, not me — I pay the Guild. So my interest is simple: the vats arrive, the driver arrives, and I'd take it kind if the guard arrives too." She glanced at the greying sky. "It's light enough. Get up, then. And cross the ford before the sun's low, both of you — that's all I'll say on it."

Tam answered with a click of his tongue and a chirrup to the oxen, and the yard gate swung shut behind the cart. The low stretch past the west gate was as bad as the landlady had promised — Thursday's rain still stood in the bowl of the road, and the near wheel went in to the hub at the worst of it. They lost the better part of an hour levering it out with the spare stave, Tam swearing steadily at the oxen, who ignored him, and the morning was half gone before the road firmed. After that the river road ran easy. Hedgerows, a roadside shrine with fresh-cut flowers, woodsmoke off a hamlet at midday. Tam drove and watched and said nothing worth saying; he ate his own sausage one-handed at a walk and let the silence sit. Past midday the land began tilting toward the water, and late in the afternoon the river showed itself — broad and brown-green, running quick, with the Reedford landing plain on the south bank: a crane, drying racks strung with dyed cloth, a walled yard. Between it and the water lay the ford, marked with stakes, and along the south bank the willow scrub came down thick and green right to the edge of the gravel. The sun was leaning on the western hills. Tam looked at it, then at the scrub, and clicked the oxen up. "Would've beat this by an hour, without the wet road. Sit tight." The cart took the water. Cold rolled off the river, the wheels found the stony shelf, and the oxen leaned into the current with their ears back. Halfway across, water white at the axles — The scrub moved. Five men rose out of it on the south bank, four with bows already at half-draw, arrowheads sloped toward the cart. The fifth stood out ahead of them at the gravel's edge, a long knife held loose in one hand, and called across the water in an easy, carrying voice. "That's far enough. Walk her in slow and tip the vats onto the bank — drivers keep their teeth, every time, so long as the dye comes out." Tam hauled back on the reins and the oxen plashed to a halt, the cart sitting broadside in the current. "Hold," he said, low, without turning his head.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
Tam answered with a click of his tongue and a chirrup to the oxen, and the yard gate swung shut behind the cart.

The low stretch past the west gate was as bad as the landlady had promised — Thursday's rain still stood in the bowl of the road, and the near wheel went in to the hub at the worst of it. They lost the better part of an hour levering it out with the spare stave, Tam swearing steadily at the oxen, who ignored him, and the morning was half gone before the road firmed.

After that the river road ran easy. Hedgerows, a roadside shrine with fresh-cut flowers, woodsmoke off a hamlet at midday. Tam drove and watched and said nothing worth saying; he ate his own sausage one-handed at a walk and let the silence sit. Past midday the land began tilting toward the water, and late in the afternoon the river showed itself — broad and brown-green, running quick, with the Reedford landing plain on the south bank: a crane, drying racks strung with dyed cloth, a walled yard. Between it and the water lay the ford, marked with stakes, and along the south bank the willow scrub came down thick and green right to the edge of the gravel.

The sun was leaning on the western hills. Tam looked at it, then at the scrub, and clicked the oxen up. "Would've beat this by an hour, without the wet road. Sit tight."

The cart took the water. Cold rolled off the river, the wheels found the stony shelf, and the oxen leaned into the current with their ears back. Halfway across, water white at the axles —

The scrub moved.

Five men rose out of it on the south bank, four with bows already at half-draw, arrowheads sloped toward the cart. The fifth stood out ahead of them at the gravel's edge, a long knife held loose in one hand, and called across the water in an easy, carrying voice.

"That's far enough. Walk her in slow and tip the vats onto the bank — drivers keep their teeth, every time, so long as the dye comes out."

Tam hauled back on the reins and the oxen plashed to a halt, the cart sitting broadside in the current. "Hold," he said, low, without turning his head.

He got the bolt off — blue light off the staff, hissing across the water — and it took the bowman in the shoulder, spinning him half around with a bark of pain. Then the riverbank came apart. The bowman didn't stay hurt and distant. He came down the gravel at a run, slung the bow, and a long blade was already out of his belt as he hit the shallows — the point went in under Alaric's ribs before he'd finished the word of his casting, a hot punch that folded him over the staff. The one with the knife was wading too, calm as a man crossing a stream to mend a fence. Two more flanked wide through the willows. Alaric dragged in air and loosed another bolt at the man bleeding on him; it struck home, tore a grunt out of him, and got nothing for it but the knife-man's guarded cut across his forearm, then the second bowman's blade opening his side. Tam was shouting something — the reins, the oxen, the cart lurching in the current — and the world was going white at the edges. The last of his breath went into a third bolt that caught the wounded man again, and then the third one stepped in off the gravel, blade first, and the cold of the river was the last thing that felt like anything. The bolt light died on the water. The staff turned over once and floated. Tam was alone on the bench with four blades around the cart, the oxen shifting and blowing, and the knife-man standing in the shallows beside the body of the Guild's mage, wiping his hand on his thigh.

The bowman didn't stay hurt and distant. He came down the gravel at a run, slung the bow, and a long blade was already out of his belt as he hit the shallows — the point went in under Alaric's ribs before he'd finished the word of his casting, a hot punch that folded him over the staff.

The one with the knife was wading too, calm as a man crossing a stream to mend a fence. Two more flanked wide through the willows. Alaric dragged in air and loosed another bolt at the man bleeding on him; it struck home, tore a grunt out of him, and got nothing for it but the knife-man's guarded cut across his forearm, then the second bowman's blade opening his side.

Tam was shouting something — the reins, the oxen, the cart lurching in the current — and the world was going white at the edges. The last of his breath went into a third bolt that caught the wounded man again, and then the third one stepped in off the gravel, blade first, and the cold of the river was the last thing that felt like anything.

The bolt light died on the water. The staff turned over once and floated.

Tam was alone on the bench with four blades around the cart, the oxen shifting and blowing, and the knife-man standing in the shallows beside the body of the Guild's mage, wiping his hand on his thigh.
